title: The Scientific Case Against Net Zero Falsifying the Greenhouse Gas Hypothesis

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper writes F = 5.35 Log(C_t/C_0) and uses base-10 log to compute 0.64-0.81°C for doubling CO2. The IPCC formula is ΔF = 5.35 ln(C/C0) with natural log; natural-log doubling gives 3.7 W/m², not 1.61 W/m². Therefore the reported temperature changes and Figure 1 are mathematically wrong and misattributed to the IPCC.

R is defined as '8.314 m³ K⁻¹ mole⁻¹ kg' but the universal gas constant is 8.314 J/(mol·K). Equation (2) T=PM/(pR) is dimensionally inconsistent with the stated P in kPa and R in SI; P must be in Pa, otherwise the computed temperature is too large by a factor of 1000.

predicted_errors.error_location: Planetary temperature calculation using the Ideal Gas Law and Table 1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The calculation T=PM/(ρR) uses the planet's observed surface pressure and density to 'predict' surface temperature. Since density is not an independent input but is obtained from or tightly coupled to the observed atmospheric temperature and pressure, the exercise is circular and cannot independently falsify the greenhouse effect.

The text states the accumulated anthropogenic contribution is '~18 ppmv (4.19ppmv p.a.)'. This is internally impossible: 4.19 ppmv/year is an annual emission rate, not an accumulated concentration. Over the industrial era, 18 ppmv would be about 0.1 ppmv/year.

The same 7-billion-person, 500 g/day calculation is first given as '~0.1638 ppmv' then as '0.1268 ppmv resting'. These are inconsistent; 1.2775 Pg CO2 corresponds to about 0.162 ppmv if all stays in the atmosphere, and the later statement that half is lost to ocean/biomass is not consistently applied.

The text says the UK 'emits about 1%' and parenthetically says '0.327 Peta grams or 0.043% of all CO2 sources'. 0.327 Pg CO2 is about 1% of global fossil-fuel CO2 emissions, not 0.043%; the two statements refer to different denominators and contradict each other without clarification.

The listed household costs £78,000 (power) + £58,000 (road transport) = £136,000, yet the text states '~£300,000 per household in total'. The £40bn/year investment to 2050 also does not obviously produce £300,000 per household; the totals are internally inconsistent.

The paper says the temperature increase 'is statistically indistinguishable from 0°K'. Kelvin is not expressed in degrees, and 0 K is absolute zero, not a temperature anomaly. This is a nonsensical unit and statistical claim.

The paper concludes 'there is an upper limit... ~0.81°C' from logarithmic absorption. But logarithmic forcing has no hard upper bound, and using the correct IPCC natural-log formula with the same λ=0.5 gives about 1.85°C for a doubling. The claimed negligible upper limit overstates the result.

The paper claims the IPCC gives '100 to 1000 years' residence time and violates the 'Principle of Equivalence'. The IPCC distinguishes molecular turnover time from perturbation lifetime; it does not simply state CO2 molecules remain 100-1000 years. The critique misrepresents the IPCC.

Numerous in-text citations have no reference entry, including Coe et al., 2021; Plimer 2009/2017/2021; Easterbrook 2016; Sasse 2021; Harde 2017a; Allmendinger 2017; Salby 2012; Statistics Norway 2023; CO2 Coalition 2023; Field 2019; and Connolly et al., 2021. A scientific-integrity review would require correction.

predicted_errors.error_location: Paragraph citing Zhong & Haigh (2013) as falsification
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Zhong & Haigh (2013) is cited among works that 'immediately falsified' the IPCC greenhouse effect. That article is an educational review explaining and affirming the CO2 greenhouse effect, so the citation does not support the claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: References to Table 1, Table 2, and Figure 2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text refers to 'Table 1' (planetary temperatures), 'Table 2' (assessments), and 'figure 2' (Keeling curve), but these are absent from the paper (only Figure 0 and Figure 1 are included). The missing items make central numerical claims unverifiable.

predicted_errors.error_location: COVID-19 and 1970s oil crisis emission sentence
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims both periods 'reduced human CO2 emissions by as much as 20%'. Global fossil CO2 emissions fell about 5-7% in 2020; they did not fall 20% during the 1970s oil crisis. The statement is factually false and overstates the test.

Figure 1 plots ΔT against CO2 concentration from 0 ppm, but the logarithmic forcing formula used to construct it is undefined at C=0 and requires a specified baseline C0. The axis/figure therefore purports to show a relationship that the underlying formula cannot evaluate at the lower bound.

The paper says the 2019 amendment committed the UK to 'a 100% reduction in emissions by 2050'. Legally it is a net-zero target: residual emissions may remain if offset by removals. Calling it a 100% emissions reduction misstates the policy.
